tips.title: Efficiency above 1 is self-diagnosing
tips.body: You cannot get more useful energy out than you put in. So an answer above 1, or above 100%, means you divided **total by useful** instead of **useful by total**. Recognise it and invert.

tips.title: Convert before you calculate
tips.body: Minutes × 60, hours × 3600, kilowatts × 1000. More marks are lost in this topic to an unconverted time than to any misunderstanding of power itself.

tips.title: Same work, sooner
tips.body: Two motors lifting the same load to the same height transfer the **same energy**. The faster one is more powerful because it takes **less time** — it does the same work sooner, not more work.

tips.title: Read the kilowatt-hour off its name
tips.body: A **kilowatt** is a power, an **hour** is a time, and power × time = **energy**. So the kilowatt-hour is a unit of energy — quicker to work out than to memorise.

tips.title: Answer with the chain
tips.body: *Lubricate it* is a third of an answer. *Lubrication reduces friction, so less is dissipated as thermal energy, so more of the input is useful and the efficiency rises* has three marks in it.

why.matters:
A kettle and a candle can both boil a mug of water. They transfer the same energy; the difference between them is **how long it takes**, and that is what power measures. It is the number stamped on every appliance and every engine because it is the thing you actually feel: the pull of a car, the wait for the kettle.

**Efficiency** is the other half: how much of what went in did the job, and how much became warmth nobody asked for. Between them they decide the size of a motor, the heat of a lamp and the cost of a bill.

examples.title: What "40 W equivalent" means on the packet
examples.body:
An LED lamp rated 5 W is sold as *40 W equivalent*: the same light as a 40 W filament bulb. The filament bulb makes light by heating a wire until it glows, so most of its 40 W leaves as thermal energy, which is why it is too hot to touch. The LED sends most of its 5 W out as light and stays cool.

Same useful output, an eighth of the input. Over 1 000 hours, the filament bulb takes $E = Pt = 40 \times 1 000$ watt-hours, 40 kWh, and the LED 5 kWh. The bill pays for the input, and the difference is the efficiency.

props.caption: The same light for a thousand hours: what each one draws from the socket.

visual.alt: Two bars drawn to scale comparing the forty kilowatt-hours a forty watt filament bulb draws over a thousand hours with the five kilowatt-hours a five watt LED draws to give the same light

examples.title: Timing yourself up the stairs
examples.body:
You can measure your own power with bathroom scales, a tape measure and a stopwatch. A 60 kg person climbing a 2.7 m flight lifts their weight through that height: $mgh = 60 \times 9.8 \times 2.7$, about 1 588 J. Run it in 4 s and that is $P = E \div t$, about 400 W.

That is where the *few hundred watts* for a person comes from. It is a fifth of a kettle and 80 LED lamps, and you cannot keep it up. A lift doing the same job in the same time has the same power.

props.caption: Power is a rate, so a short burst up the stairs is a fifth of a kettle.

visual.alt: Three bars drawn to scale comparing a two thousand watt kettle, a person running up a flight of stairs at about four hundred watts, and a five watt LED lamp

examples.title: Why heating a petrol car is free
examples.body:
A petrol engine is about 30% efficient: of every 100 J in the fuel, 30 J moves the car and 70 J becomes thermal energy in the engine. There is so much of it that the car carries a radiator just to throw it away. The cabin heater simply borrows some on the way to the radiator, so on a cold morning it costs nothing.

An electric motor is about 90% efficient, so it has only 10 J of waste heat to spare. Heating an electric car has to draw on the battery instead, and the range drops in winter.

steps.title: What power means
steps.body:
**Power is the rate at which energy is transferred**, or equivalently **the rate at which work is done**.

The word **rate** means *per second*, and that is the whole idea: power is not how much energy, it is **how fast** the energy is moved.

$$P = \frac{E}{t} \qquad\qquad P = \frac{W}{t}$$

- **P** — power, in **watts, W**
- **E** — energy transferred, in **joules, J**
- **W** — work done, in **joules, J**
- **t** — time, in **seconds, s**

The two equations are the same equation. **Work done is energy transferred** — they are two names for the same quantity, measured in the same unit.

**The definition of the watt:**

$$\textbf{an energy transfer of 1 joule per second} = \textbf{a power of 1 watt}$$

**The illustration the spec asks for.** Compare two electric motors that both lift the **same weight** through the **same height**, but one does it **faster**.

- Both transfer the **same energy**, because the job is identical.
- The faster one has the **greater power**, because it transfers that energy in **less time**.

So a more powerful motor does not do *more* work — it does the **same** work **sooner**. That distinction is exactly what power means, and it is the one the exam tests.

steps.title: Rearranging, and getting the units right
steps.body:
With three quantities there are three forms:

$$P = \frac{E}{t} \qquad E = P t \qquad t = \frac{E}{P}$$

**The unit traps are where the marks go, and there are three:**

**Time must be in seconds.** A question giving a time in minutes or hours is testing exactly this. Two minutes is **120 s**; half an hour is **1800 s**.

**Kilowatts are not watts.** 1 kW = **1000 W**. A 2.5 kW kettle is a **2500 W** kettle.

**The kilowatt-hour is a unit of energy, not power.** It is the energy transferred by a power of one kilowatt in one hour — so it is a power multiplied by a time, which is an energy. It appears on electricity bills because the joule is inconveniently small for household use.

**A useful check.** Power tells you joules **per second**. So if you calculate a power and the number seems enormous — a million watts for a light bulb — you have probably left a time in minutes or hours. If it seems tiny, you have probably multiplied where you should have divided.

**Typical powers**, worth knowing so that an answer can be sanity-checked:

- an LED lamp: about 5 W
- a person climbing stairs: a few hundred watts
- a kettle: about 2000 to 3000 W
- a car engine: tens of thousands of watts

steps.title: Efficiency
steps.body:
**Efficiency** is the fraction of the energy supplied that is transferred **usefully**.

$$\text{efficiency} = \frac{\text{useful output energy transfer}}{\text{total input energy transfer}}$$

It can also be calculated from **powers**, and this second form is just as examinable:

$$\text{efficiency} = \frac{\text{useful power output}}{\text{total power input}}$$

**You must be able to recall and apply both.**

**Why both work.** Power is energy per second, so dividing one power by another divides one energy by another with the seconds cancelling. The **ratio is what matters**, not the units — which is why a machine transferring 60 J out of 100 J and one delivering 600 W out of 1000 W are both 60% efficient.

**As a decimal or as a percentage.** Efficiency has **no unit**, because it is one energy divided by another. You may be asked for it either way:

- as a **decimal**: 0.8
- as a **percentage**: multiply by 100, giving 80%

Read the question. If it asks for a percentage and you give 0.8, you lose the mark for the sake of one multiplication.

**Efficiency can never be more than 1, or 100%.** If your answer is, you have divided the wrong way round. Conservation of energy makes an efficiency above 1 impossible: you cannot get more useful energy out than you put in.

**And it is never exactly 1 either**, because every real change dissipates some energy.

steps.title: Increasing efficiency
steps.body:
**This part is Higher tier.** You should be able to **describe ways to increase the efficiency** of an energy transfer.

The logic is always the same, and it is worth stating explicitly because it turns a memory test into a reasoning one:

$$\textbf{efficiency rises when less energy is dissipated}$$

Since the input is fixed and *input = useful + dissipated*, **anything that reduces the dissipation increases the useful output**, and so the efficiency. So to answer any question of this kind: find what is dissipating energy, and reduce it.

| What dissipates energy | How to reduce it | So |
|---|---|---|
| friction between surfaces | lubricate with oil or grease | less is dissipated as thermal energy |
| air resistance | streamline the shape | less is dissipated in the air |
| electrical resistance | use thicker wires | less heating for the same current |
| energy escaping a building | add thermal insulation | a lower rate of transfer out |
| sound from a machine | tighten and mount the parts better | less energy carried away as sound |

**Answer with the chain, not just the cure.** *Lubricate it* is a third of an answer. The full one names **the cure**, **what it reduces**, and **the effect on efficiency**:

> *Lubricating the moving parts reduces the friction between them, so less energy is dissipated as thermal energy, so more of the input is transferred usefully and the efficiency increases.*

That sentence has three marks in it.

**And no machine can reach 100%.** The spec says energy is dissipated *in all system changes*. So a question asking whether a design could be made perfectly efficient has one answer: **no** — and the reason is conservation together with the fact that every real change dissipates something.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Power is a rate, so the same job done faster needs more power.** Two motors lifting the same load to the same height transfer the **same energy** — the job is identical. The faster one is more powerful because it does that work in **less time**. Answers that say the faster motor *does more work* have missed the definition.

**Efficiency has no unit, because it is a ratio.** One energy divided by another, or one power divided by another. That is also why both forms of the equation give the same answer: in the power form the seconds cancel. A machine giving 60 J out of 100 J and one giving 600 W out of 1000 W are equally efficient.

**Efficiency above 1 is impossible, and it tells you what you did.** You cannot get more useful energy out than you put in without creating energy. So an answer above 1, or above 100%, means you divided **total by useful** instead of **useful by total**. It is a self-diagnosing error — recognise it and invert.

**Efficiency of exactly 1 is impossible too.** Energy is dissipated in **all** system changes, so there is always something on the wasted side. A question asking whether a design could reach 100% is answered **no**, and the reason is that every real change dissipates energy — not that the engineering is imperfect.

**Answer efficiency questions with the chain.** Cure, what it reduces, effect: *lubricating the parts reduces friction, so less energy is dissipated as thermal energy, so more of the input is useful and the efficiency rises.* Three marks in one sentence, and it works for every cure in the table.

**The unit traps are worth more marks than the physics.** In this topic more marks are lost to minutes left unconverted and kilowatts read as watts than to any misunderstanding of power itself. Convert first, then calculate: it costs ten seconds and saves the question.

**The kilowatt-hour is energy.** A kilowatt is a power and an hour is a time, and power multiplied by time is energy. Recognising that from the **name** of the unit is quicker and more reliable than remembering which it is.

**Sanity-check with a typical value.** A domestic lamp is a few watts to a hundred; a kettle is a couple of thousand. If your lamp comes out at a million watts, look for a time left in minutes before you look for anything else.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Power is the rate at which energy is transferred**, or the rate at which work is done.
- $P = \dfrac{E}{t}$ and $P = \dfrac{W}{t}$ — **work done is energy transferred**.
- Power in **watts**, energy in **joules**, time in **seconds**.
- **An energy transfer of 1 joule per second is a power of 1 watt.**
- Rearranged: $E = Pt$ and $t = \dfrac{E}{P}$.
- **Convert first**: minutes × 60, hours × 3600, kilowatts × 1000.
- The **kilowatt-hour** is a unit of **energy** — a power multiplied by a time.
- Two motors doing the same job transfer the **same energy**; the faster one has the **greater power**.
- $\text{efficiency} = \dfrac{\text{useful output energy transfer}}{\text{total input energy transfer}}$
- Or from powers: $\dfrac{\text{useful power output}}{\text{total power input}}$ — **recall both**.
- Efficiency has **no unit**. Multiply by 100 for a percentage, and read which the question wants.
- Efficiency **cannot exceed 1**, or 100%. If it does, you divided the wrong way round.
- Efficiency is **never exactly 1**, because energy is dissipated in **all** system changes.
- **To increase efficiency, reduce the dissipation**: lubrication, streamlining, thicker wires, insulation.
- Answer with the **chain**: the cure, what it reduces, and the effect on efficiency.

questions.prompt: A crane lifts a load, transferring 60 000 J of energy in 40 s. Its motor is supplied with 100 000 J in that time. Calculate the crane's power output and its efficiency, and describe two ways the efficiency could be increased.
questions.solution: The useful power output is found from the useful energy transferred and the time taken. Power equals energy transferred divided by time, so the useful output power is sixty thousand joules divided by forty seconds, which is one thousand five hundred watts. The efficiency is the useful output energy transfer divided by the total input energy transfer, so it is sixty thousand divided by one hundred thousand, which is 0.6, or sixty per cent as a percentage. This is less than one, as it must be, because energy is dissipated in all system changes and so no machine can be completely efficient. The forty thousand joules that were not transferred usefully have been dissipated to the surroundings and stored in less useful ways, mostly as thermal energy in the motor, the cable and the surrounding air, and some as sound. The efficiency could be increased in two ways. Lubricating the moving parts of the crane, such as the bearings and the pulleys, would reduce the friction between them, so less energy would be dissipated as thermal energy and a greater proportion of the input would be transferred usefully, raising the efficiency. Using thicker wiring in the motor circuit would reduce the electrical resistance, so less energy would be dissipated as thermal energy in heating the wires for the same current, again leaving more of the input available for lifting the load.

questions.modelAnswer:
**Power output.** $P = \dfrac{E}{t} = \dfrac{60\,000}{40} = 1500$ W.

**Efficiency.** $\dfrac{60\,000}{100\,000} = 0.6$, or **60%**. Less than 1, as it must be, since energy is dissipated in **all** system changes.

**Where the other 40 000 J went.** Dissipated to the surroundings and **stored in less useful ways** — mostly thermal energy in the motor, cable and air, and some as sound.

**Two ways to increase it — each with the full chain:**

- **Lubricate the bearings and pulleys.** This reduces **friction**, so less energy is dissipated as thermal energy, so a greater proportion of the input is transferred usefully and the efficiency rises.
- **Use thicker wiring in the motor circuit.** This reduces **electrical resistance**, so less energy is dissipated heating the wires for the same current, leaving more available to lift the load.

**What separates a full answer** is that chain — the cure, what it reduces, and the effect — rather than naming cures on their own.

questions.prompt: Explain what power means, and explain why two motors that lift the same load to the same height can have different powers.
questions.solution: Power is defined as the rate at which energy is transferred, or equivalently the rate at which work is done. The word rate means per second, so power is not a measure of how much energy is involved but of how quickly that energy is moved. It is calculated as the energy transferred divided by the time taken, and it is measured in watts, where an energy transfer of one joule per second corresponds to a power of one watt. Two motors that lift the same load through the same height are doing exactly the same job, so the work done, and therefore the energy transferred usefully, is the same for both. If one motor completes the lift in a shorter time, then it has transferred that same quantity of energy over a smaller interval, and since power is energy divided by time, a smaller time with the same energy gives a larger power. For example, if each motor transfers three thousand joules, but one takes ten seconds and the other takes thirty seconds, the first has a power of three hundred watts and the second a power of one hundred watts, so the faster motor is three times as powerful. The key point, and the one most often misunderstood, is that the more powerful motor does not do more work. It does exactly the same work, but sooner. This is precisely what it means for power to be a rate.

questions.modelAnswer:
**Power is the rate at which energy is transferred**, or the rate at which work is done. **Rate means per second**: power measures not how much energy but **how quickly** it is moved.

$$P = \frac{E}{t}$$

measured in **watts** — an energy transfer of **one joule per second** is **one watt**.

**Why two motors differ.** Lifting the same load through the same height is **the same job**, so the work done, and the energy transferred, is the **same** for both. If one takes less time, then in $P = E/t$ the energy is unchanged and the time is smaller — so the power is **greater**.

With 3000 J each: $\dfrac{3000}{10} = 300$ W against $\dfrac{3000}{30} = 100$ W. The faster motor is **three times** as powerful.

**The point most often misunderstood**, and the one that earns the last mark: the more powerful motor does **not do more work**. It does exactly the **same** work, **sooner**. That is what it means for power to be a rate.

examTechnique.body:
Define power as the rate at which energy is transferred, or the rate at which work is done.

Convert times into seconds and kilowatts into watts before calculating anything.

Divide useful by total when finding efficiency, and check the answer is below 1.

Read whether the question wants a decimal or a percentage.

Give efficiency no unit.

When comparing two machines doing the same job, say the energy is the same and only the time differs.

When describing how to increase efficiency, name the cure, what it reduces, and the effect on efficiency.

Check a power answer against a typical value before writing it down.
examinerErrors: Leaving a time in minutes or hours.
Dividing total input by useful output, giving an efficiency above 1.
Giving a decimal when the question asked for a percentage.
Writing a unit after an efficiency.
Saying the faster of two motors does more work.
Treating the kilowatt-hour as a unit of power.
Naming a way to increase efficiency without saying what it reduces.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer treats power as a rate and can say what follows: two motors doing the same job transfer the same energy, and the faster one is more powerful because the time is smaller. It knows efficiency is a ratio with no unit, that both the energy form and the power form give the same answer because the seconds cancel, and that an efficiency above one is not a strange result but a sign the division was inverted. It explains that no machine can reach 100% because energy is dissipated in all system changes, rather than blaming the engineering. And it answers every efficiency question with the full chain: the cure, what it reduces, and the effect.
